CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Music — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the music club habit: one steady beat, a family echo game, and permission for every pot in the cupboard to be an instrument for ten minutes.

What is this?

Music club is regular sound play — clapping, singing, kitchen drums — where the goal is a felt beat, not a performance. The card’s printed skills are Rhythm & Sound: the steady pulse underneath music and the many ways things can vibrate.

What does it mean?

Keeping a steady beat trains the same timing the body uses for walking, cutting and swinging. Echo games train listening memory — hearing a pattern and holding it in the head is early math wearing a song’s clothes.

What does the child need to know?

Two clapping hands, a pot and a wooden spoon, and one song everybody likes. A shaker (rice in a sealed bottle) adds a second voice to the family band.

Why this matters

Rhythm play is one of the strongest predictors of early reading — syllables live on beats. Music sessions also teach turn-taking naturally: you play, then I play.

What it teaches

Steady-beat keeping, listening memory, loud/soft and fast/slow contrast words, turn-taking, and the confidence that comes from making a sound nobody stops.

Words to learn

beatrhythmloudsoftfastslowechoshakertempo

Say this to your child

“"Music club is open! First we find the beat — clap with me, one two one two. Now you are the leader, I will echo everything you play. Ready?"”

Step by step

  1. Clap the steady beat while a song plays — pat knees if clapping is too loud.
  2. Play echo claps: three-beat patterns, child echoes, then swap leader roles.
  3. Explore loud and soft with the pot drum: thunder hands, mouse hands.
  4. March the beat around the room — big steps for loud, tiptoes for soft.
  5. Finish with one song sung together, then one minute of silence to hear the difference.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the player’s fingers spread across a small keyboard — pianos show the pattern of music visually, low notes on the left walking down, high on the right climbing up.

Ask your child

"Is this music loud or soft?" "Can your feet keep the beat?" "What did my pattern sound like?" "What in this kitchen could join the band?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may keep a beat with surprising accuracy, invent a two-note song with real words in it, or drum on every surface in the house — the last one is called practice.

Out in the real world

Musicians, dancers, surgeons and baristas all rely on rhythm — steady timing is the hidden skill behind espresso shots and heartbeats alike.

Try it together

Kitchen orchestra: assign every player one object (pot, shaker, spoon-glass), pick a steady beat, and conduct loud and soft with big and small hand waves. The conductor gets to end the piece with a fist — silence at last.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we call the steady pulse?" (the beat) "Show me soft hands on the drum." "What happens when I clap a pattern?" (we echo it back)

This lesson pairs with the Music flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
